LOCAL KNOWLEDGE
What a Lake Worth Beach Bathroom Remodel Actually Involves

The parts of the job that are specific to this city, and that decide whether a project runs on schedule or waits on someone else's calendar.

Six historic districts, and why your bathroom probably still clears them

Lake Worth Beach adopted its preservation ordinance in 1996 and has since designated six local historic districts and four individually significant structures, with review overseen by the volunteer Historic Resources Preservation Board. That is a far wider footprint than most Palm Beach County cities, so a real share of homes here sit inside one.

The useful detail is what the rule actually covers. The city says a Certificate of Appropriateness is required before exterior work begins and before a building permit can be issued for a property in a district. A bathroom is interior, so most remodels here never touch that process. The moment a project adds or changes a window, alters an exterior door, or vents through an outside wall, it does. We establish which side of that line your project falls on at the walkthrough.

The permit rules changed on July 1, 2026, and the headline is misleading

Under Florida House Bill 803, certain residential projects valued under $7,500 can now qualify for a building permit exemption. That has been widely repeated as "you do not need a permit any more," which is not what it says.

Two things matter. The city states plainly that the exemption is not automatic: owners must apply for and receive approval before any work begins. And $7,500 is well below what a full bathroom renovation costs, so on the work we do the threshold rarely comes into play at all. The city has also created a standalone Zoning Permit process for certain site improvements, and its Planning & Preservation Division still checks zoning, landscaping, tree protection and historic requirements where they apply. We handle the permitting process either way.

Older houses hide their problems behind the tile

The building stock that makes this city's historic districts worth protecting also means many bathrooms sit on plumbing and framing that predate every current standard. We routinely open walls here and find cast iron waste lines at the end of their life, galvanized supply, no useful blocking, and a circuit never sized for a modern bathroom.

None of that is a reason to avoid the project, but it is a reason to price it honestly. We would rather look at what is behind the wall during the walkthrough and put the real number in the estimate than discover it on day three and hand you a change order.

Permit procedures, preservation regulations, and building codes change. Everything above reflects the city's published information as of August 2026, and we reconfirm current requirements on every project.

LOCAL CONDITIONS

What a Palm Beach County Kitchen Has to Handle

Most of what decides a kitchen layout here is under the floor or written into the building, not on the drawing.

Almost every home in this county sits on a concrete slab. There is no basement and no crawlspace, so moving a sink, a range, or an island is not a matter of running new lines beneath the floor. It means cutting the slab, rerouting under it, and pouring back. That single fact often decides whether an island can go where you want it, and it is the first thing worth checking before a layout is settled.

Salt air and year-round humidity are hard on the parts of a kitchen people touch. Hinges and pulls corrode faster within a few miles of the water. Interior humidity swings move solid wood more than they would inland, so panel construction and finish choice matter more here than the door profile does.

A large share of Palm Beach County kitchens sit in condos or association communities. That usually means an approval packet before anything is demolished, a service elevator that has to be reserved, and working hours set by the building rather than by the crew. Those constraints shape a schedule as much as scope does, which is why we ask about them at the first walkthrough. We wrote up the details boards actually approve if you want to see what gets reviewed.

Impact-rated windows and doors limit what can move. Openings are structural, and the header and surrounding wall are not something to reroute casually around a new sightline. Where a window cannot move, the layout works around it, and it is better to know that at design than at demolition.

MATERIALS

Cabinetry, Countertops, and Finishes

Most of what separates one kitchen remodel from another is decided before demolition starts.

Cabinet box construction

The box carries the weight of the kitchen, so what it is built from matters more than the door style on it. Plywood boxes hold hardware better over time and move less through humidity swings than particle board. Interior fittings, drawer count, and door profile get chosen after the layout is settled, not before.

Countertops and seam placement

Quartz, quartzite, and marble each behave differently. Quartz is the most forgiving day to day. Natural stone gives you veining no engineered slab reproduces, and asks for sealing and some care in return. Where the seams fall matters as much as the material, so slab layout is decided before fabrication rather than at install.

Islands and waterfall edges

A waterfall edge only reads as intentional when the veining is carried around the corner, and that is a slab selection made early. Islands also carry plumbing and electrical that the slab dictates, so size and position get confirmed against what is actually under the floor before the cabinetry is ordered.

Backsplash and large-format tile

Large-format porcelain removes grout lines but is unforgiving of a substrate that is not flat. The wall has to be trued before the first piece goes up, and the layout is dry-set so cuts land where they are least visible. A slab backsplash carries the countertop material up the wall and needs the same seam planning.

Hardware and fixtures

Unlacquered brass patinas, and near the coast it does it faster. That is either the point or a problem depending on the homeowner, so it is worth deciding deliberately rather than discovering in year two. Finish families are chosen across the whole room at once, so the faucet, the pulls, and the lighting agree with each other.

Lighting in layers

A kitchen needs more than a ceiling fixture. Task light under the uppers, something deliberate over the island, and general light that does not flatten the room. Because it is all set during rough-in and inspected there, lighting is one of the few things that is genuinely expensive to reconsider later.

LOCAL KNOWLEDGE
What a Boca Raton Kitchen Remodel Actually Involves

The parts of the job that are specific to this city, and that decide whether a project runs on schedule or waits on someone else's calendar.

The hood is what turns a kitchen into an exterior job

A kitchen renovation is an interior project right up until the range hood needs somewhere to go. Ducting a hood outside means a cap through a wall or a roof, and that is a change to the outside of the building.

In a community with architectural review, an exterior penetration is exactly the kind of thing that gets looked at, even though the rest of the kitchen never would. It is the single most common way a Boca kitchen quietly acquires a second approval, and it is worth settling at design rather than on the day the duct is run.

Gated communities have their own front door

A large share of Boca Raton's housing sits inside gated and country-club communities, and those come with a process before anyone touches the house: contractor registration, proof of insurance, gatehouse access for the crew, and permitted working hours.

For a kitchen this matters more than it does for most rooms, because the deliveries are large. Cabinetry arrives in a single load and stone slabs arrive on a frame. Both need a delivery window, a route in, and somewhere to stage. We confirm what your community requires as part of writing the scope rather than discovering it the morning the truck arrives.

The panel is often the real limit, not the layout

A modern kitchen asks a lot of a house electrically. Induction, double ovens, a dedicated circuit for the microwave drawer, another for the wine refrigerator, and lighting on more than one control.

In older housing stock the existing service can be at its limit before any of that is added. That is a load calculation question, and it belongs at design, because the answer occasionally changes the appliance package or adds a service upgrade to the scope. Finding out at rough-in is the expensive version.

Three trades, three sub permits, staged inspections

Boca Raton runs building permits through its Development Services department across two systems: applications, fees and inspection scheduling in Boca eHub, and plan review uploaded through Boca ePlans.

A full kitchen is not one permit and one inspection. Moving plumbing, altering electrical, and ducting a hood each bring their own sub permit and their own inspection point, and they have to clear in sequence before finishes go on. That sequence is the schedule. We handle the permitting process and coordinate the inspections so the order holds.

Permit procedures, community requirements, and building codes change. Everything above reflects published information as of July 2026, and we reconfirm current requirements on every project.

LOCAL KNOWLEDGE
Four Things to Know Before a Boynton Beach Kitchen Starts

What the city's own rules say about a kitchen, and where condominium and single-family projects go different ways.

The city names kitchens on its permit list

Some homeowners hope a kitchen can be done as a cosmetic refresh without the city involved. Boynton Beach answers that directly. Its permit FAQ lists kitchen and bathroom remodels among the typical projects that require a permit, alongside new circuits, electrical panels, and gas lines.

The same FAQ says what does not need one: painting, flooring, similar finish work, and swapping a plug-in appliance. It even lists cabinetry as permit-free, but only when it is not part of a kitchen or bathroom remodel. A new state exemption for small single-family jobs, in effect since July 2026, leaves out plumbing, electrical, gas, mechanical, and structural work, which is most of what a real kitchen involves. We handle the permitting process so the job is on record from the start.

A condo kitchen is filed as a commercial project

This one surprises people. In SagesGov, the city's permitting system, the residential project type covers single-family homes and townhouses. Apartments and condos sit under the commercial project type, even when the work is one kitchen in one unit.

It matters because the city says that if the wrong project type is selected, the application is abandoned and has to be filed again, and payments cannot be moved across. On top of the city's side, the building has its own rules: work hours, elevator reservations, where debris goes, and whether a range hood can vent outside or has to recirculate. We confirm all of it with the association before a layout is drawn.

Decide where the sink goes before anything is submitted

Boynton reviews the whole project inside SagesGov, from plan review through inspections and close-out. Its own guidance notes that a change to proposed work can only go in as a revision after the permit has been approved and issued.

In a kitchen, that makes the early decisions expensive to reverse. Moving the sink to the island, shifting the range to an outside wall, or adding a circuit for a second oven all change the drawings. So we settle the layout, the appliance list, and the lighting plan with you first, and only then prepare the package. A kitchen that changes shape halfway through costs time twice: once in rework, and again in review.

Historic review stops at the outside wall

Boynton's Historic Resources Preservation Board reviews designated historic buildings and sites. Under the city's criteria, a Certificate of Appropriateness covers actions affecting the exterior of a designated property, and of any property inside a designated district.

An interior kitchen renovation is generally not what that review looks at. It becomes relevant when the design reaches outside: a larger window over the sink, a new door to the patio, or a hood vent cut through an exterior wall. If your property carries a designation, we raise those items during design so they can be reviewed before the schedule depends on them.

Everything above comes from the City of Boynton Beach's published pages as checked in September 2026. Permit procedures and codes change, and we reconfirm them with the city before each project.

LOCAL KNOWLEDGE
What a West Palm Beach Kitchen Remodel Actually Involves

The parts of the job that are specific to this city, and that decide whether a layout is buildable at all.

In a tower, the hood may have nowhere to go

This is the question that quietly decides a condominium kitchen. Ducting a range hood to the outside is usually not something an individual unit can do in a high-rise, because the exterior of the building is not yours and there may be no route through it.

What remains is a dedicated building shaft where one exists, or a recirculating hood. That is not a small detail: it influences the range you can sensibly specify, where the cooking surface can sit, and how the ceiling is built above it. We confirm it with the building before a layout is drawn, because designing a cooking wall that cannot vent is the most expensive way to find out.

The countertop has to fit in the elevator

Stone arrives as a slab, and a slab is large, heavy and rigid. In a house it comes through a door. In a tower it goes in a service elevator, and the elevator has dimensions.

Where those dimensions are tighter than the run of countertop you want, the answer is a seam, and the useful move is deciding where that seam falls rather than leaving it to the fabricator on install day. A seam placed at a sink or a corner reads as intentional. A seam placed in the middle of an island reads as a compromise. This gets settled during templating.

The original kitchen was a back room, not the heart of the house

In the older neighborhoods the kitchen was designed as a small service room at the rear, closed off from the living space, often with a separate pantry and its own outside door. That is what the plan gave you and it is not how anyone lives now.

So the actual project is usually not a kitchen renovation, it is opening the kitchen to the room next to it. That crosses from finishes into structure: whether the wall carries load, what beam replaces it, and the engineering and inspection that follow. It is very doable and it is a different scope, a different permit path, and a different number than a like-for-like kitchen.

Check the zoning and permits before you draw

West Palm Beach reviews and permits construction through its Development Services Building Division, and permits run through EPL, the city's Civic Access portal. The division also publishes a research tool that checks a proposed project against zoning code and indicates which permits it will need.

That is worth using at the start rather than the end. On a kitchen the answer usually confirms the routine path, but where the project touches structure or the exterior it can surface a requirement that changes the sequence. We handle the permitting process and carry the review and inspections through the project.

LOCAL CONDITIONS

What a Palm Beach County Bathroom Has to Handle

In a bathroom, the drain and the building decide more than the drawing does.

Homes here are built on concrete slabs, so the existing drain location is a real constraint rather than a starting suggestion. Moving a toilet or a shower drain means cutting the slab, rerouting under it, and pouring back. It is routine work, but it is not free, and it is the difference between a layout that can be built and one that only looks good on paper.

That same slab decides whether a curbless shower is possible. A zero-entry pan needs depth for the slope to the drain, and that depth has to come from somewhere. Sometimes it is available and sometimes the floor has to be built up across the room to get it. Either way it is worth answering early, because it changes the door, the threshold, and the tile layout.

Condo bathrooms carry an extra layer. Waste stacks and risers are shared with the units above and below, so how far a wet wall can move is often set by the building rather than by the design. Add an approval packet before demolition, a reserved service elevator, and building hours, and the schedule is shaped before the first tile is chosen. We wrote up the details boards actually approve.

Then there is the air. Year-round humidity puts real load on waterproofing and ventilation, and coastal air is hard on fixtures. A bathroom that was detailed for a dry climate will show it here, usually first at the fan, the grout, and the hardware.

MATERIALS

Waterproofing, Tile, and Fixtures

A bathroom is judged on its finishes and fails on what is behind them.

Waterproofing comes first

Everything visible in a shower sits on top of a waterproofing layer that nobody will ever see. It is the part of the job with the least to show for it and the most riding on it. Pan slope, corners, curbs, and every penetration get detailed before tile, because this is the one layer that cannot be corrected later without taking the room apart.

Curbless and zero-entry showers

A curbless shower has to drain without a curb to contain it, which puts all the responsibility on the slope and the drain. A linear drain lets the floor fall in one direction instead of four and makes large-format tile far easier to keep flat. It is the detail that makes a shower feel considered rather than simply step-free.

Large-format tile and slab walls

Fewer grout lines means fewer places for a wall to hide its flaws. Large panels need a trued substrate, a dry layout so cuts fall where they are least visible, and enough hands to set a sheet without flexing it. Carried floor to ceiling, it is the single biggest change you can make to how finished a bathroom reads.

Natural stone in a wet room

Marble is beautiful and it etches. In a shower or around a vanity it will record what it meets, which some homeowners like and others do not. Sealing schedule, honed against polished, and where the stone actually goes are decisions worth making with clear eyes rather than discovering after the first year.

Glass, fixtures, and hardware

Frameless glass is measured after the tile is set, not before, because it is cut to the room as built. Unlacquered brass patinas quickly in coastal air, which is either the intent or a surprise. Fixture finishes are chosen as a family so the shower, the vanity, and the hardware are speaking the same language.

Ventilation that is actually sized

The exhaust fan is the least glamorous decision in the room and the one that protects everything else in it. Sized to the space and ducted properly, it keeps humidity off the paint, the grout, and the hardware. Undersized or vented poorly, it quietly undoes good tile work over a few seasons.

What a Boca Raton Bathroom Remodel Actually Involves

The parts of the job that are specific to this city, and that decide whether a project runs smoothly or stalls.

Permits go through Development Services

Boca Raton runs building permits through its Development Services department, on two separate systems. Applications, fees, inspection scheduling, and public records live in Boca eHub. Drawings and permit files are uploaded for plan review in Boca ePlans, the city's ProjectDox portal.

A bathroom remodel that moves plumbing, alters electrical, or changes framing needs a permit and the associated sub permits. We handle the permitting process and carry the job through inspections. Worth knowing if you are considering pulling a permit yourself: on a single-family owner-builder permit, the city requires the property owner to complete the sub permit applications personally.

Condo and HOA approval comes before demolition

Much of Boca Raton's housing stock sits inside condominium associations and HOA-governed communities, and those boards approve work on their own calendar, not yours.

A typical packet wants the scope in writing, the contractor's insurance naming the association as certificate holder, and sometimes a plumbing riser detail if you are relocating fixtures. Buildings also set work hours, restrict weekend and holiday work, require the service elevator to be reserved and padded, and dictate how debris leaves the property. We build the approval window into the schedule from the start rather than treating it as a surprise.

Wind-borne debris rules, if the bathroom has an exterior window

Palm Beach County sits inside Florida's Wind-Borne Debris Region. It is not the High-Velocity Hurricane Zone, which covers only Miami-Dade and Broward, but opening protection requirements still apply here.

For most bathroom remodels this never comes up. It matters when a bathroom has an exterior window and the design calls for changing it, enlarging it for light, or swapping obscured glass. At that point the window becomes a code-governed opening rather than a finish choice, and it needs to be permitted and specified accordingly. We flag this during design, not after demolition.

The housing stock is not one thing

Boca Raton spans 1920s Mizner-era architecture in Old Floresta, mid-century ranch homes in neighborhoods like Camino Gardens, country club communities such as Broken Sound, and waterfront estates in The Sanctuary and Royal Palm Yacht & Country Club.

Those homes hide very different things behind the wall. Cast iron waste lines and galvanized supply in the older stock, slab-routed plumbing in the mid-century houses, and stacked wet walls with shared risers in the condo towers. We open a wall expecting to find the era's problems rather than assuming the plans tell the whole story.

Boynton Beach runs a preservation program built around designated buildings and sites. Its Historic Resources Preservation Board oversees locally or nationally designated properties, the formal program was adopted in 2011, and it has held Certified Local Government status since 2012.

The decisions that make a bathroom age well are structural, they happen at framing, and they are nearly free at that moment. Solid blocking behind the wall where a grab bar might one day go. A door opening wide enough to matter. A shower whose entry does not depend on stepping over anything.

Retrofitting any of it later means opening finished tile, which is the expensive version of the same conversation. We ask the question during design even when nobody has raised it, because saying no to blocking costs nothing and saying yes later costs a wall.

Close to the Intracoastal and the ocean, corrosion is not theoretical. Hinges, pulls, shower hardware, and exposed valve trim all live in a room that is humid by design and salty by geography.

That shapes finish selection more than people expect. Unlacquered brass will patina quickly here, which is either the intended look or an unwelcome surprise. Ventilation matters more too: an exhaust fan sized to the room and ducted properly is what keeps the humidity off the paint, the grout, and the hardware, and it is the least glamorous line on the estimate.

LOCAL KNOWLEDGE
How a Palm Beach Gardens Bathroom Remodel Moves From Plan to Permit

What the city's own process means for a bathroom project here, and where the real delays tend to come from.

A Palm Beach Gardens address is not always a Palm Beach Gardens permit

A mailing address is not how the city answers the question of whether a home is inside its limits. Its planning FAQ tells owners to look up the property on the Property Appraiser's site and read the municipality field. If it says Palm Beach Gardens, the home is inside the municipal boundary and the city's Building Division reviews the work.

If it names another jurisdiction, the permit, the forms, and the inspectors all change. We look up the parcel before we write a scope, because building a submittal for the wrong office is the kind of mistake that costs weeks and teaches nothing.

Your association's letter can become part of the city file

The Building Division's residential remodel checklist sends plans through two tracks: the building trades (structural, mechanical, plumbing, gas, electrical) and Development Compliance. That second track checks construction plans against the city's land development regulations and the conditions of approval in any development order that applies to the property.

The same checklist lists an HOA approval letter, required when the plan reviewer asks for it. In a city where many homes sit inside master associations, we treat that letter as part of the submittal, not an afterthought. Getting the association's approval first means a reviewer's request is answered the day it arrives.

Plans are submitted as signed PDFs, and the signature matters

Palm Beach Gardens moved its permitting online. The city no longer takes printed documents larger than letter size, large plans go in as PDF files only, and every contractor has to register in the system.

Most bathroom remodels only need trade plans. When a project moves a wall or needs an architect's or engineer's drawings, the city requires those plans to be digitally signed by that professional, and it warns that a self-signed file can significantly slow processing. We confirm which documents a scope needs, and who signs them, before the package is assembled.

Inspections run in order, and the final waits on the rest

A bathroom collects inspections as it goes: plumbing rough-in, electrical rough, and equipotential bonding where it applies, all before the walls close. The city books them through its portal and states that the final inspection is only available once the earlier ones have passed.

That sequence is why our schedule has inspection dates written into it rather than hoped for. Requests made before 3 p.m. can be booked for the next day, so a well-run job loses very little time between stages. A missed inspection, on the other hand, can mean opening finished tile to show what is behind it.

The historic board calendar runs in months, not weeks

West Palm Beach maintains 18 locally-designated historic districts and 46 individually-designated sites. That second number is the one people miss.

A large share of West Palm Beach bathrooms sit in condominium buildings, and in a tower the waste stack and risers are shared with the units above and below. They are not yours to move.

That sets a hard limit on how far a toilet or a shower drain can travel, which in turn decides whether the layout you want is buildable at all. Building access, elevator reservations, and permitted work hours then shape the sequence around it.

In the older two-story housing stock, an upstairs bathroom is governed by what is under the floor. A drain line needs consistent fall to run, and the depth available for it is set by the joists, which are not adjustable.

This is what usually decides whether a curbless or zero-entry shower is possible on a second floor, and it is worth answering before anyone falls in love with a layout. Sometimes the depth is there. WHY HOMEOWNERS CALL US
One Team, the Whole Bathroom

A large primary bathroom gives you more freedom, and it also gives a mistake more places to hide. A long walk-in shower needs a floor that is sloped correctly along its whole length, and a double vanity wall needs plumbing that is laid out on purpose, not inherited from the last remodel.

We handle the whole thing in house: demolition, plumbing, electrical, waterproofing, tile, glass, cabinetry, and finish work. The same crew runs it from the first day to the walkthrough.

Stone, glass, and custom vanities are where a large bathroom is judged. Those go to the people who do them well.

LOCAL KNOWLEDGE
What a Wellington Bathroom Remodel Actually Involves

How the village handles this kind of project, and which of its boards and rules actually touch a bathroom.

Wellington does not take paper plans

The village's Building Department processes permits electronically and nothing else. The application goes in by email, the drawings are uploaded to ProjectDox as individual, digitally signed pages, and fees are paid through a separate self-service portal before the file is released for review.

When a reviewer leaves a comment, each one marked unresolved needs a written answer before the file moves again. We handle the permitting process, and most of the work is done before the upload: drawings that answer the obvious questions, product documentation in the right folder, and a plan that matches the bathroom that will actually be built.

Why the new exemption will not cover your bathroom

Wellington's page on House Bill 803, in effect from July 1, 2026, lists what the exemption excludes: electrical, gas, plumbing, structural, and mechanical work, projects partly or wholly in a flood hazard area, and jobs split into smaller pieces to avoid a permit. Even qualifying work has to be applied for.

A real bathroom remodel moves drains and supply lines and adds circuits, so it sits outside that list on the first line. Even exempt work, the village notes, still has to meet the building code, zoning, floodplain rules, and HOA requirements. We plan every renovation as permitted, inspected work from the first drawing.

The boards that sound relevant, and the one that is

Wellington has an Architectural Review Board that meets on the fourth Wednesday of each month. Its published duties cover approved materials, designs, and color charts, appeals on those, and plans for multifamily and non-residential development. None of those duties is written around the inside of a single-family bathroom.

The Equestrian Preserve Committee is an advisory board on land use in the Equestrian Preserve Area, including flooding and drainage. For a bathroom, the approval that usually shapes the start date is your community association's. We confirm which rules apply to the property at the walkthrough, then sequence the work around them.

Inspections on the village's clock

Village inspectors work Monday through Friday, 7 AM to 3:30 PM, and inspections can be booked by text. After-hours and weekend inspections are possible on request when the village has availability, which makes them an exception, not a plan.

A bathroom is inspected before its walls close, so the order matters. We schedule rough plumbing and electrical inspections into the week before tile, not the week after, and we arrange gate access and a contact on site so an inspector is never turned away at the entrance of a gated community or a farm.

Permit procedures, board duties, and building codes change. Everything above reflects the Village of Wellington's published information as of September 2026, and we reconfirm current requirements on every project.

Home Remodeling Services in Palm Beach County

Five services, run by one crew: kitchens, bathrooms, tub-to-shower conversions, custom closets, and built-in millwork. This page sets out what each one covers, so you know what is in the number before you sign anything.

START HERE

Where the Scope Lines Fall

Almost nobody calls us wanting to buy a service. They call because a room does not work, and the fix rarely sits neatly inside one category.

A kitchen that needs a new island usually needs the lighting moved. A primary bath that gains a walk-in shower usually gives up a tub, and often the closet next to it gets rebuilt while the wall is already open. So the useful question is not which service you need. It is where the work starts, where it stops, and who is responsible for the parts in between.

That is what the rest of this page answers. Each service below lists what is actually included, because a scope you can read is the only defense against a price that moves after demolition. If the answer turns out to be most of the house, that is a whole-home renovation and it is planned differently. If you would rather just talk it through, request a consultation and we will walk the space with you.

Kitchen remodel · Palm Beach Gardens

WHAT EACH SERVICE COVERS

Five Services, One Accountable Crew

Most projects combine two or three of these. All of them are run by the same team that walks your home on day one.

01 · KITCHENS

Kitchen Remodeling

The largest projects we run, and the ones where layout matters more than finishes. Before choosing a door style we work out whether the island can grow, whether the range can move, and what the range hood needs in order to vent. Those three answers set the budget more than any material selection does.

Layout planning, measured drawings, and a written scope
Cabinetry, countertops, islands, and backsplash
Appliance fit, range hood venting, and lighting layout
Plumbing and electrical rough-in coordinated and inspected
Tile, trim, paint, and the final punch list

02 · BATHROOMS

Bathroom Remodeling

A bathroom is a small room with the highest concentration of things that can go wrong later. The parts that decide whether it lasts are the ones you never see again: the pan, the waterproofing, and how the tile is set over it. We build those first and photograph them before they are covered.

Fixture relocation, including moving a toilet or shower drain
Shower pan, waterproofing, and large-format tile
Vanities, counters, mirrors, and frameless glass
Exhaust, lighting, and heated floor where the layout allows
Finish carpentry, paint, and the final walkthrough

03 · CONVERSIONS

Tub-to-Shower Conversion

The most contained project on this list, and the one most often finished in a single stretch. It suits a guest bath with a tub nobody has filled in years, and a primary bath where the tub is taking floor space a proper shower would use better. The drain usually has to move, which is the part that decides the schedule.

Tub removal and drain relocation to the new shower position
New pan, curb or curbless entry, and full waterproofing
Tile, niche, bench, and frameless glass
Valve and shower system replacement
Grab-bar blocking set in the wall while it is open

04 · CLOSETS

Custom Closets

Built as millwork rather than assembled from a catalogue kit cut down to fit. That distinction shows up in the corners, at the ceiling line, and anywhere a wall is out of plumb, which in this county it usually is. We measure the opening you have and build to it.

05 · MILLWORK

Built-Ins and Millwork

Media walls, bookcases, window seats, and the cabinetry that makes an awkward wall useful. Built on site to the wall you actually have, with the wiring and venting solved before the carpentry closes it in. This is also where a lot of kitchen and living-room projects quietly end up.

Most are more than one. We will tell you which at the walkthrough.

Request a Consultation

THE COMMON SPINE

In Every Project, Whatever the Room

These are not upgrades and they are not line items you add. They are how the work is run.

A Written Scope

Measured drawings and a fixed estimate before anything is torn out. If it is not written down it is not in the price, which cuts both ways and is the point.

Selections Made With You

Cabinetry, counters, tile, fixtures, and lighting chosen together, with the combinations that photograph well but live badly pointed out before you buy them.

The Permitting Process

We handle the permitting process and prepare the approval packet your city, building, or association requires, then track it through to approval.

Protection and Cleanup

Floor and stair protection laid through the whole path our crew uses, dust control at the work area, and the site left clean at the end of each day.

Rough-In and Inspection

Plumbing and electrical rough-in coordinated in the right order and inspected at each stage, rather than discovered to be wrong once the tile is on.

Finish Work and Punch List

Trim, paint, hardware, and the small corrections that decide how the room reads. We do not call the project done until you walk it and agree.

BEFORE ANYTHING IS TORN OUT

How a Project Gets Scoped

Four steps, all of them before you have committed to anything. The build sequence comes after, and you get it in writing first.

1

We walk the space with you and measure it, and you tell us what is not working about it today rather than what you think the fix is.

2

We say out loud which of the five services your project actually touches, and where it will run into something structural, shared, or governed by an association.

3

You get a written scope and a fixed estimate, with the allowances named so they cannot quietly grow once demolition starts.

4

Selections are finalized and the approval packet goes in. Only then does a demolition date go on the calendar.

TWO SERVICES, ONE PROJECT

Kitchen and Built-Ins, Run Together

Cabinetry that carries from the kitchen through to the living space, set by the same crew in one sequence rather than by two companies six weeks apart.

IN PRACTICE

Projects That Travel Together

Four combinations we quote most often, and why the second half is cheaper while the wall is already open.

Primary Bath and Closet

They usually share a wall. Rebuilding the closet while the bathroom is stripped means one protection setup, one crew mobilization, and one punch list instead of two.

Kitchen and Living-Room Millwork

Open-plan homes read as one room, so cabinetry that stops at the kitchen edge looks like it stopped. Running the built-ins in the same phase keeps the finish and the sight lines consistent.

Guest Bath Conversion, Then Primary

Converting the guest bath first gives you a working shower to live with while the primary is out of service. It is a sequencing decision more than a budget one, and it is worth making early.

Whole Floor, One Permit Cycle

If two or three rooms are on the list within a year, scoping them together usually means one approval cycle instead of two, which in a condo or an association is the part that takes the longest. At that point it is a whole-home renovation, and the order the rooms happen in matters more than the list.

LOCAL CONDITIONS

What Palm Beach County Adds to a Remodel

Four things that change the scope here and would not come up in the same project inland or up north.

Slab-on-Grade Plumbing

Most homes here sit on a slab, so moving a toilet or a shower drain means cutting concrete rather than working from below. It is entirely doable and it is not a surprise, but it belongs in the estimate rather than in a change order, and it is the single most common reason a bathroom scope moves.

Salt Air on Hardware

Within a few miles of the water, finish choices that behave perfectly elsewhere pit and spot here. We steer hinges, slides, shower hardware, and exposed fittings toward finishes that survive coastal air, because the alternative is a room that looks tired in two seasons.

Condo and Association Windows

A great many projects here are governed by a board rather than only by the city, and boards meet on their own calendar. Some restrict work to certain months entirely. Knowing your association's submission deadline before selections are locked is what keeps a project from waiting a full cycle.

WHOLE-HOME RENOVATION

Whole-Home Renovation in Palm Beach County

Several rooms, one plan, one crew, one sequence. The hard part of renovating a whole house is not any single room. It is the order the rooms happen in and what overlaps with what.

Call (561) 269-9658
Request a Consultation
Insured
Palm Beach County
One Crew, One Schedule

WHAT WE MEAN BY IT

Several Rooms, Treated as One Project

A whole-home renovation here means the interior of the house reworked together: the kitchen, the bathrooms, the closets, and the millwork that ties them to each other.

It is the same work we do one room at a time, run as a single project instead of four separate ones. That changes the sequencing, the budget order, and how long any part of the house is out of use. It does not change the trades involved.

Being plain about the boundary is more useful than being vague about it. This is interior renovation. Where a project needs work on the structure of the building or its outside envelope, that is outside what we take on, and you will hear that at the walkthrough rather than after you have signed something. What we own is the design, the selections, the cabinetry and millwork, the tile and finish work, and the schedule that holds all of it together.

If you are weighing one room against several, the services page sets out what each one includes on its own.

One language of detail, carried room to room

THE CASE FOR ONE PLAN

What Changes When the Rooms Are Planned Together

Four things get cheaper or better when the whole interior is one project rather than four. None of them are about materials.

One Mobilization

Protection laid once through the whole path the crew uses, one set-up, one clean-down. Done as four projects you pay for that four times, and live through it four times.

One Approval Cycle

Where a building or an association has to sign off, submitting the whole interior once usually means one cycle instead of several. In a condo that is often the longest single item on the schedule.

Decisions That Agree

Choosing the kitchen floor without knowing the hall floor is how houses end up with four good rooms that argue with each other. Selections made as a set do not need to be reconciled later.

One Number, Written Down

A measured scope across every room, priced together, before demolition. Four separate quotes over three years is four chances for the price to reset and for the finish to drift.

Thinking about more than one room?
We will walk the house and tell you what is worth doing together.
Call (561) 269-9658
Request a Consultation

THE ORDER MATTERS MORE THAN THE LIST

How a Whole-Home Project Is Phased

There is a right order, and it is mostly decided by plumbing and by which rooms you cannot lose at the same time.

1

Every room measured and scoped in one pass, so the plan is built on the whole floor rather than on the room we happen to be standing in.

2

Selections locked across all rooms together. Long-lead cabinetry and stone are ordered first because they set the dates everything else hangs off.

3

The permitting process handled for the whole scope at once, and the approval packet your building, HOA, or city requires prepared before anything is torn out.

4

A guest bathroom first wherever the layout allows, so the house keeps a working shower while the primary is out of service.

5

Wet rooms next. Anything that moves a drain through the slab happens before floors go down, not after.

6

Kitchen after that, in the stretch you have planned to live around, with a temporary setup agreed in advance rather than improvised.

7

Closets and built-in millwork last, because they scribe to finished walls, but designed at the very start so the wiring and blocking are already in place.

8

Floors, trim and paint carried through as one pass, then a single punch list for the whole house rather than four.

THE PART NOBODY ASKS UNTIL LATER

Living in the House While It Happens

Most people stay. It is workable, and it is much more workable when the phasing was designed around it from the start.

Keep One Bathroom

The single most useful constraint you can give us. Say which bathroom you cannot lose and we sequence around it, rather than discovering the problem in week three.

Plan the Kitchen Gap

You will be without a working range and sink for a defined stretch. You get that number at the estimate, and a temporary arrangement agreed before the cabinets come out.

Contain the Dust

The work zone is sealed and the route in and out is protected. A whole-home project without that discipline makes the parts of the house you are still living in unusable.

Or Phase It Over Years

Some clients plan the whole interior once and then build it in stages as budget allows. That works, and it works far better with one plan behind it than with four unrelated quotes.

PALM BEACH GARDENS

The Kitchen, Set Against the Rest of the House

Cabinetry, stone and lighting chosen so the room reads as part of the home rather than the newest thing in it.

ROOM TO ROOM

The Same Standard in Every Room

A whole-home project is only as good as its least considered room. These are the three that usually prove it.

Go deeper by room: kitchen remodeling, bathroom remodeling, custom closets, built-ins and millwork, or see the full gallery.

LOCAL CONDITIONS

What Palm Beach County Adds at This Scale

The same four constraints that shape a single room, except a whole-house project meets all of them at once instead of one at a time.

Slab-on-Grade, Repeatedly

Most homes here sit on a slab, so every relocated drain means cutting concrete. On one bathroom that is a line item. Across a kitchen and three bathrooms it is a sequencing decision, and it is the main reason the wet rooms come before the floors.

A Longer Association Window

A whole-interior scope is a bigger submission than a single room, and some buildings restrict work to certain months entirely. On a multi-month project that calendar, not the trades, is usually what sets the start date.

Salt Air on Every Finish

Within a few miles of the water, hardware and exposed fittings that behave elsewhere pit and spot here. Choosing consistently across the whole house matters more than in one room, because a mismatch shows up as some rooms ageing faster than others.

Access, Multiplied

In a tower, every stone slab has to fit the service elevator, which dictates seam placement before anyone picks a material. Loading-dock hours and protected corridors turn into a real constraint when the same route carries months of deliveries.

GOOD QUESTIONS

Whole-Home Renovation Questions
How long does a whole-home renovation take?

It depends on how many rooms, how much plumbing moves, and how quickly selections and any board approvals clear. What you get at the estimate is a dated sequence rather than a single number, so you can see which parts of the house are affected when. If a date moves you hear it from us rather than noticing it.

Can we do it in stages instead of all at once?

Is it one contract or one per room?

CUSTOM CLOSETS · PALM BEACH COUNTY

Custom Closets, Built Into the House

Walk-in closets and dressing rooms built as millwork rather than assembled from catalogue parts. Designed, built, and finished by the same crew that runs the rest of the renovation.

THE DIFFERENCE

Millwork, Not a Kit

Most closet companies sell a system. Standard box widths, standard hanging heights, a catalogue of components assembled on site and scribed to fit as best they can. It works, and for a lot of houses it is the right answer.

We build closets the way we build the rest of a renovation: as cabinetry made for the room it is going into. That means the depth suits what you actually own, the drawer banks land where you reach for them, and the run terminates against the wall properly instead of with a filler strip.

It also means the closet can be part of a larger project. If the primary suite is being renovated anyway, the closet is built in the same sequence, by the same crew, with the same finish carpentry standard as the cabinetry in the bathroom next to it.

That is the honest distinction, and it is worth understanding before you get quotes. A system is faster and usually costs less. Millwork fits the house and matches everything else in it.

WHAT'S INCLUDED

What a Custom Closet Project Covers

A complete closet build, handled in house from the first measurement to the last drawer pull.

1

Measurement, inventory of what actually needs storing, and layout

2

Demolition of existing shelving and wire systems

3

Framing corrections, blocking, and any wall or ceiling repair

4

Electrical for integrated and cabinet lighting, where the design calls for it

5

Cabinetry: hanging sections, drawer banks, shelving, and shoe storage

6

Islands, benches, and seating in rooms with space for them

7

Hardware, mirrors, valet rods, and glass or panelled doors

8

Paint, trim, flooring transitions, and final finish carpentry

MATERIALS AND CONDITIONS

What a Closet Has to Handle Here

A closet is a small room with no ventilation and a lot of fabric in it, which in this climate is worth designing around.

Humidity is the real design constraint

A closed closet in Palm Beach County holds still, humid air against wool, leather, and silk. That argues for ventilated door panels or a louvred section rather than a sealed box, and for not pushing a hanging run tight against an exterior wall where condensation is most likely.

Panel construction, not just door style

Solid wood moves more here than it does inland, so how a panel is built matters more than what it looks like. Plywood carcases hold hardware and stay square through seasonal swings. The visible surface can be anything; the box underneath is what decides whether the drawers still run true in five years.

Two wardrobes, not one

Many houses here are lived in part of the year, which means the closet is holding a resort wardrobe and a stored one at the same time. That changes the ratio of long hang to double hang and the amount of enclosed, dust-protected storage worth building.

Lighting that shows the actual colour

Getting dressed under a single ceiling fixture means judging navy against black in the wrong light. Integrated shelf and rod lighting at a sensible colour temperature is the difference, and because it is wired during rough-in it is one of the few decisions that is genuinely expensive to add later.

Condos and what the building allows

In a condominium the closet is usually the least regulated room in a renovation, because nothing structural or shared is being touched. The constraints that remain are logistical: elevator reservations, work hours, and getting long cabinetry components into the unit at all.

Hardware you will touch every day

Drawer slides, hinges, and rods are the parts that fail first and the parts you interact with most. Near the coast, finish choice on exposed hardware matters for corrosion as much as for looks, and undermount soft-close slides are worth the difference over side-mount.

CONFIGURATIONS

Three Ways a Closet Gets Laid Out

Most closets fall into one of three shapes. Which one you have decides where the drawers go and how much of the run can be hanging.

Custom Built-Ins and Entertainment Centers

THE DIFFERENCE

Built Into the Room, Not Bought For It

A piece of furniture sits in front of a wall. A built-in becomes the wall. That difference is mostly invisible in a photograph and completely obvious standing in the room, because a built-in is scribed to the ceiling, returns into the corners, and carries its own lighting and power.

It is also the reason built-ins are worth doing during a renovation rather than after one. The wiring, the blocking, and the ventilation all get decided while the wall is open, which is when they are nearly free.

We build media walls, library and display walls, window seats, banquettes, mudroom and laundry cabinetry, and the cabinetry that flanks a fireplace. Same crew, same finish standard as the kitchen.

If you are weighing a built-in against a good freestanding piece, the honest test is whether the wall is awkward. Sloped ceilings, a chase in the wrong place, an off-centre fireplace, a room that is not square: those are the situations where a built-in earns its cost.

WHAT'S INCLUDED

What a Built-In Project Covers

Everything from the blocking behind it to the last piece of trim.

1

Measurement, elevation drawings, and layout against the room as built

2

Demolition of existing millwork, mantels, or shelving

3

4

5

Ventilation and cable routing for AV components inside cabinetry

Cabinetry, shelving, and the display or media surround

7

Integrated lighting, hardware, and glass or panelled doors

8

Paint, trim, scribing, and final finish carpentry

WHAT DECIDES THE RESULT

The Parts You Only Get One Chance At

Most of what separates a built-in that looks original to the house from one that looks added is settled before the cabinetry arrives.

Heat is the thing people forget

AV equipment inside a closed cabinet generates heat and shortens its own life. Ventilation, whether passive vents or a small managed fan, is planned with the cabinetry rather than drilled in afterwards. It is invisible when it is done properly and obvious when it is not.

Power and data before drywall

Outlets behind the screen, a conditioned circuit for equipment, and data or conduit for whatever replaces today's hardware. Running conduit now costs very little; fishing a cable through a finished built-in later means opening it up.

Nothing in the room is square

Walls bow, ceilings slope, and floors run out of level, which is why a built-in is scribed on site rather than simply set in place. The joint where the cabinetry meets the ceiling and the corners is where the eye goes, and it is entirely a finish carpentry problem.

Screen height, not screen size

The most common regret is a screen mounted too high because the design started with the fireplace rather than with the seating. Where the sofa sits decides the centre line, and that decides the whole elevation. Worth settling on paper before anything is built.

Lighting the shelves, not the room

Display lighting is what makes a library or media wall read as architecture instead of storage. Integrated shelf lighting is wired during rough-in, so like everything else here, it is a decision that is cheap now and expensive later.

Coastal air reaches inside cabinets

Hinges, slides, and exposed hardware corrode faster within a few miles of the water, and interior humidity swings move solid wood more than they would inland. Panel construction and hardware finish are chosen for that, not just for looks.

OTHER WAYS TO USE THE WALL

Beyond the Media Wall

A media wall is the most common version of this. It is not the only one, and the same millwork approach solves several other awkward walls.

Planning a renovation in that room anyway?
Built-ins cost far less when the wiring and blocking happen while the wall is open.

Is a built-in worth it over a good freestanding piece?

It depends on the wall. If the room is square, the ceiling is flat, and a well-made piece of furniture fits, furniture is the cheaper and more flexible answer. WHO WE ARE
One County, One Crew

H&H Signature Renovations is a custom residential remodeler based in Lake Worth Beach, working the length of Palm Beach County. Our shop sits in the middle of the territory we serve, which is deliberate: it keeps our crew on job sites rather than on I-95.

We stay inside a radius we can actually cover. A contractor who takes work three counties wide ends up managing logistics instead of building, and the client feels it in the schedule. Everything on this page is within an hour of our door.

Founded and led by Tristan Dankert, H&H owns the project from first walkthrough to final reveal. We are insured in Florida, and we provide documentation to your association or property manager whenever a building requires it before work can begin.

WHAT WE BUILD
Services We Offer Across the County

Full-scope residential remodeling. We do not take on small-repair or maintenance work.

Kitchen Remodeling

Cabinetry, stone, appliance integration, lighting, and the layout changes that make the room actually work.

Bathroom Remodeling

Complete bathroom remodels, from relocating fixtures to tile, glass, vanities, and finish carpentry.

Whole-Home Renovation

Multi-room and full-house projects, sequenced so trades follow each other properly and the schedule holds.

Custom Closets

Custom Cabinetry and Built-Ins

Millwork made for the wall it lands on: bars, media walls, banquettes, and storage that reads as architecture.

Tile and Flooring

Large-format tile, stone, and wood, set with the substrate prep that decides whether it still looks right in ten years.

WORKING IN THIS COUNTY
What Changes From One Address to the Next

Palm Beach County is not one jurisdiction. It is dozens of them, and the rules that govern your remodel are set by which side of a city line your house sits on.

Your city, not the county, usually issues the permit

Each municipality here runs its own building department, with its own submittal portal, its own review queue, and its own way of staging inspections. A remodeler who works one city and assumes the rest match learns otherwise on the first project.

Boca Raton, for example, permits through its Development Services department across two systems: Boca eHub for applications, fees, inspection scheduling, and records, and Boca ePlans, the city's ProjectDox portal, for uploading drawings for plan review. Neighboring cities do it their own way. We work out the specific path for your address before we build the schedule, not after the drawings are done.

Wind-borne debris region, and what it is not

Palm Beach County sits in the Wind-Borne Debris Region, so exterior openings carry impact-protection requirements that shape any remodel touching windows, doors, or sliders. If your scope moves an opening or changes its size, that requirement follows it.

What the county is not is the High Velocity Hurricane Zone. HVHZ covers Miami-Dade and Broward only. It matters because product approvals and details written for HVHZ are stricter than what applies here, and a bid built on the wrong assumption is either over-priced or, worse, not what your inspector is looking for.

Paperwork that has to be right before anyone swings a hammer

Florida Statute 713.13 requires a Notice of Commencement to carry the property's legal description, street address, and tax folio (PCN) number. Palm Beach County's Building Division states plainly that incomplete NOCs get returned for completion and re-recorded.

That is a week lost to a form, on a job that had not started yet. It is the least interesting part of a renovation and one of the most common places a schedule slips, so we handle the recording and confirm it is clean before the crew is scheduled.

Associations set the calendar as often as the city does

A large share of the housing here sits under an HOA, a condo association, or a country club community with its own architectural review. Those bodies meet on their own schedule, and no amount of urgency moves a board meeting.

So we treat approval as a scheduled phase rather than a formality: scope documentation prepared up front, certificates of insurance naming the association, and the work planned around the building's rules on hours, elevator use, and debris removal. Building that window into the timeline at the start is the difference between a delay and a plan.

Permitting specifics above are current for Boca Raton as published by the city. Requirements differ by municipality, and we confirm the process for your specific address before quoting a schedule.
